content.body: Have you ever needed to quickly find if a word exists in a grid of letters? That's exactly what we'll learn to do efficiently. We'll discover how to search for words in a 2D grid using a clever remembering technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
1. Apply a backtracking search to explore all possible paths in a grid.
2. Implement a visited tracking system to avoid reusing the same cell.
3. Explain why we need to mark cells as visited during the search.
4. Combine backtracking with boundary checking to solve the word search problem.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a small example. Look at this 2x2 grid and try to find the word 'AB'. Can you trace a path starting from any cell?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: Can you find 'AB' in this grid?
content.successMessage: Great! You found it by moving from A to B (right or down).

content.title: Try a bigger grid
content.successMessage: Well done! You traced a path like A→B→C (right twice).

content.title: One more challenge
content.successMessage: Excellent! You found the path A→B→F→E (right, down, left). Notice how you couldn't reuse cells you already visited.

content.body: What you just did was explore possible paths in the grid, checking adjacent cells to build the target word. You intuitively avoided going back to cells you already used in your current path.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the grid gets larger (like 10x10) and words get longer, manually tracing every possible path becomes impossible. We need a systematic method that remembers where we've been in each search path. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we have already seen in our current search path. We'll use a data structure to track visited cells so we don't accidentally reuse them. Think of it like leaving breadcrumbs on cells we've visited in our current path, then picking them up when we backtrack.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use depth-first search with backtracking. For each starting cell, we'll explore all four directions, marking cells as visited during the current search and unmarking them when we backtrack.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Searching for 'AB' in [[A,B],[C,D]]:
1. Start at (0,0)='A', mark visited
2. Check right (0,1)='B', matches next letter
3. Found complete word 'AB'
4. Backtrack: unmark (0,1), then (0,0)
Key: We mark visited to avoid reusing cells in same path.

content.body:
1. For each cell in the grid, start a search if first letter matches
2. Use recursive function to explore up/down/left/right
3. Mark current cell as visited before exploring neighbors
4. If word is fully matched, return true
5. Unmark cell when backtracking
6. Return false if no path found from current cell
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the main function
steps.instruction: Start by creating the main function that will search for the word. We'll call it exist and it should take the board (2D array) and word (string) as parameters.
steps.hint: Remember to define the function with two parameters.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function declaration with correct parameters
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the main function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you have both parameters: board and word.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function called exist that takes board and word.

steps.title: Add the DFS helper function
steps.instruction: Inside the exist function, create a helper function called dfs. It should take row, column, and index parameters. The index tracks our position in the word.
steps.hint: Define dfs inside exist. It needs to know board and word too.
steps.expectedOutcome: A nested dfs function with three parameters
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The dfs helper is ready to be implemented.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Check that dfs has row, col, and index parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: dfs needs row, col, and index to track position.

steps.title: Add base cases to dfs
steps.instruction:
In the dfs function, add the base cases:
1. If index equals word length, we found the word (return true)
2. If out of bounds, return false
3. If current cell doesn't match word[index], return false
steps.hint: Check boundaries first, then character match.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! All base cases are correctly handled.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're getting there. Make sure all three conditions are checked.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: we need to check word completion, boundaries, and character match.

steps.title: Mark visited and explore directions
steps.instruction: After the base cases, we know the current cell matches. Mark it as visited by changing its value, then explore all four directions. Remember to store the original character first.
steps.hint: Use a temporary variable to store board[row][col] before marking.
steps.expectedOutcome: Visited marking and directional exploration implemented
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the core backtracking logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Check that you're marking visited and exploring all directions.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: mark visited, explore 4 directions, then restore the cell.

steps.title: Add the main loop
steps.instruction: Now complete the exist function by adding a loop that tries dfs from every cell in the board. If dfs returns true from any starting cell, return true. Otherwise return false.
steps.hint: Use nested for loops to iterate through all rows and columns.
steps.expectedOutcome: Complete exist function with main loop
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've completed the full implementation.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're calling dfs with index 0 and returning the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check: loop through all cells, call dfs(row, col, 0), return true if any succeeds.

steps.title: Test with an example
steps.instruction: Let's test our function. Create a test case with a 3x3 board and search for the word 'ABC'. Add console.log to see the result.
steps.hint: Call exist with a sample board and word, then log the result.
steps.expectedOutcome: Test case added and function called
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your implementation correctly finds 'ABC' in the grid.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. Make sure you're calling exist and logging the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create a test board, call exist(board, word), and log the result.

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented the Word Search algorithm using backtracking with visited tracking. Key takeaways:
1. We use DFS to explore all possible paths in the grid
2. Marking cells as visited prevents reusing them in the same path
3. Restoring cells when backtracking allows exploring alternative paths
4. The 'notebook' metaphor helps remember what we've seen in our current search
Remember: always check boundaries and character matches before exploring further!
content.title: Done
